title: Geometry-calibrated equilibrium sensing for inverse design of nonlocal topological photonic lattices
abstract: Topological photonic lattices are commonly designed using short-range Hamiltonians, yet realistic nanophotonic structures are governed by geometry- and wavelength-dependent long-range electromagnetic interactions. Here we introduce a geometry-calibrated quantum equilibrium-propagation framework for inference and inverse design in finite nonlocal plasmonic Su-Schrieffer-Heeger lattices. A two-qubit equilibrium sensor is trained in effective-coupling space to distinguish boundary-localized from trivial finite-lattice responses. Because labels inherited from the nearest-neighbor SSH model become unreliable in the presence of nonlocal hopping, each sample is independently relabeled using nonlocal winding numbers and a finite-gap criterion. On this physics-verified evaluation set, the sensor achieves 99.8% sensitivity and 98.1% specificity. A physics-gated robustness score then ranks verified configurations by boundary response, response contrast, gap stability and compatibility with the selected nonlocality regime. Full-wave extinction spectra of isolated and paired gold nanoparticles establish a geometry-to-coupling calibration linking particle size and separation to wavelength-resolved pair couplings. Projecting this calibration onto the verified coupling landscape identifies a finite plasmonic geometry supporting spectrally distinct corner- and edge-dominated responses at 546 and 642 nm, with sector-to-bulk intensity contrasts of $2.4 \times 10^{4}$ and $1.5 \times 10^{3}$, respectively. The framework links realistic electromagnetic geometry to nonlocal topological design, moving beyond nearest-neighbor design rules with physics-verified, geometry-resolved inference.
summary: This paper introduces a quantum equilibrium-propagation framework to enable the inverse design of nonlocal topological photonic lattices. It overcomes the limitations of nearest-neighbor models by incorporating full-wave electromagnetic interactions derived from plasmonic structures. The method rigorously verifies topological phases using winding numbers and identifies specific physical geometries that yield desired, strong boundary-localized optical responses.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of inverse design for topological photonic lattices, moving beyond simplified nearest-neighbor models to incorporate realistic, long-range electromagnetic interactions.
main_result: A novel framework was developed that successfully links realistic electromagnetic geometry (via full-wave simulation) to physically verified, nonlocal topological design, identifying specific geometries supporting distinct boundary responses.
method: The approach combines a geometry-calibrated quantum equilibrium-propagation (QEP) sensor with rigorous physical verification using nonlocal winding numbers and finite-gap criteria.
model_or_system: The system involves finite nonlocal plasmonic Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) lattices constructed from gold nanoparticles. The model incorporates long-range, geometry- and wavelength-dependent electromagnetic couplings.
key_observables: Boundary-localized vs. trivial responses (measured by QEP sensor), nonlocal winding numbers, finite-gap criterion, and boundary-to-bulk intensity contrast.
important_parameters: Wavelength ($\lambda$), particle size, separation gaps ($g_1, g_2$), and the nonlocality regime ($\eta_{	ext{NL}}$).
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that the QEP sensor, when coupled with physical relabeling, can accurately map complex electromagnetic geometry to topological invariants and measurable boundary responses.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the framework components, including the comparison between ideal and nonlocal SSH models, the QEP sensor mapping, the necessity of physical relabeling using winding numbers, and the final mapping of geometry to distinct spectral responses.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem (nonlocal interactions), develops the QEP sensing framework, implements a physics-gated relabeling procedure using winding numbers, calibrates the geometry-to-coupling relationship using full-wave simulations, and finally applies the inverse design to find target geometries.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it provides a concrete, physics-informed methodology for designing quantum optical structures where interactions are not simple nearest-neighbor hopping, bridging quantum topology with applied electromagnetism.
